profession_name: Low Vision Therapists, Orientation and Mobility Specialists, and Vision Rehabilitation Therapists

daily_reality.summary: These professionals help people with vision loss maximize their remaining vision, navigate environments safely, and regain independence. They work in hospitals, rehabilitation centers, schools, and client homes. Critical workforce shortage — fewer than 600 CVRTs in the entire US.
typical_tasks: Assess functional vision and determine rehabilitation needs
Teach orientation and mobility techniques (cane travel, GPS navigation)
Prescribe and train patients on low vision optical devices (magnifiers, telescopes)
Teach adaptive living skills (cooking, reading, personal care)
Modify home and work environments for visual accessibility
Train clients on assistive technology (screen readers, magnification software)
Collaborate with ophthalmologists and occupational therapists
daily_reality.seasonality: Steady demand year-round. School-year creates peaks for pediatric services. Aging population ensures growing demand.

regulatory.summary: ACVREP provides professional certification (CLVT, COMS, CVRT). State licensure varies. Medicare/Medicaid cover certain services. ADA and IDEA mandate services for persons with disabilities.

key_laws.name: IDEA
key_laws.description: Ensures vision services in schools for children with disabilities

key_laws.name: Rehabilitation Act Section 504
key_laws.description: Prohibits discrimination against persons with disabilities

key_laws.name: State licensure requirements
key_laws.description: Varies by state; some require specific O&M or rehabilitation licensure

requirements: Master's degree in vision rehabilitation, O&M, or related field
certifications: COMS — Certified Orientation and Mobility Specialist
CATIS — Certified Assistive Technology Instructional Specialist

regulatory.penalties: State licensing violations. Liability for inadequate mobility training leading to injury.

tools.summary: Low vision optical devices, assistive technology, mobility aids, and environmental modification tools.

primary_tools.description: Primary mobility aid for O&M training

primary_tools.name: Screen magnification software (ZoomText, MAGic)
primary_tools.description: Computer access for low vision users

primary_tools.name: Screen readers (JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver)
primary_tools.description: Computer and mobile access for blind users

secondary_tools: Adaptive kitchen and daily living devices
Eye charts and functional vision assessment tools
pain_points: Limited awareness of services among referring physicians
Insurance coverage gaps for rehabilitation services
High travel burden for home-based services
Rapid technology changes requiring constant learning

terminology.summary: Specialized terminology blending ophthalmology, rehabilitation, and assistive technology fields.

terms.O&M: Orientation and Mobility — teaching safe independent travel
terms.ACVREP: Academy for Certification of Vision Rehabilitation & Education Professionals
terms.low vision: Visual impairment not correctable by standard glasses/surgery
terms.legal blindness: Visual acuity ≤20/200 or visual field ≤20 degrees
terms.functional vision: How a person uses their remaining vision in daily life
terms.eccentric viewing: Technique using peripheral retina when central vision is lost
terms.sighted guide: Technique for walking safely with a sighted companion
terms.trailing: Using hand contact with walls/surfaces for orientation
terms.landmark: Permanent object used for orientation reference
terms.CCTV: Closed Circuit Television — video magnification system
terms.AMD: Age-related Macular Degeneration — leading cause of vision loss in elderly
terms.TVI: Teacher of the Visually Impaired (school setting)
terms.deafblind: Combined hearing and vision loss requiring specialized services
terms.wayfinding: Process of navigating from one location to another
terms.daily living skills: Adaptive techniques for cooking, cleaning, personal care

career_psychology.summary: Meaningful rehabilitation career with salary range $55K-$121K. Critical workforce shortage creates strong demand. 23.8% job growth projected. Deep satisfaction from restoring independence to vision-impaired individuals.
career_path: Master's degree in Vision Rehabilitation / O&M
fears: Isolation as sole specialist in an organization
Keeping up with rapid assistive technology changes
motivation: Directly restoring independence and quality of life
Working one-on-one with clients in meaningful ways
Critical shortage means high demand and job security
Making a tangible difference in daily functioning
Diverse work settings (clinic, home, community, schools)
burnout_factors: Emotional weight of working with newly vision-impaired individuals
Small field with limited peer support

community.summary: Small but dedicated professional community organized around ACVREP for certification, AER for education, and various blindness organizations.

associations.name: ACVREP
associations.description: Certification body for vision rehabilitation professionals

associations.name: Association for Education and Rehabilitation of the Blind and Visually Impaired (AER)

online_communities: Facebook O&M and vision rehab groups

market.summary: Critical workforce shortage (fewer than 600 CVRTs nationally). 23.8% projected growth driven by aging population and AMD prevalence. 31,000 new jobs projected. Salary $55K-$121K.
market.growth_rate: 23.8% projected (well above national average), 31,000 new jobs
top_employers: VA Healthcare System (largest employer of vision rehab professionals)
Schools for the blind and mainstream school districts
market_trends: Critical nationwide shortage of qualified professionals
Aging baby boomers driving AMD-related demand explosion
Assistive technology advances requiring new training
Growing awareness of vision rehabilitation services
